items.excerpt: Robert Kiyosaki had two dads: one earned a PhD yet worried about money his whole life, the other never finished eighth grade yet became one of the richest men in Hawaii. This book is about the difference between two ways of thinking. We've broken it into ten lessons even elementary-school kids can follow, each with both Chinese and English versions.
items.text: Robert Kiyosaki had two dads: one earned a PhD yet worried about money his whole life, the other never finished eighth grade yet became one of the richest men in Hawaii. This book is about the difference between two ways of thinking. We've broken it into ten lessons even elementary-school kids can follow, each with both Chinese and English versions. Robert Kiyosaki had two dads. One earned a Ph.D. and worried about money his whole life. The other never finished eighth grade and became one of the richest men in Hawaii. This book is about the difference between their two ways of thinking. We rebuilt it as ten lessons a primary-school student can follow, each in Chinese and in English. This is a reading course, not investment advice. The concrete trades in the book happened in America decades ago; the rules, markets, and risks all differ from today's, and the author himself keeps saying 'what I did isn't a recommendation for you.' We only learn how he thinks, and every exercise stays in everyday life — no real buying or selling involved. This is a reading course, not investment advice. The book's deals happened in America decades ago, under different rules, markets and risks — the author himself keeps saying he does not recommend them. We only borrow his way of thinking. Every exercise here happens in daily life, never in real trading. items.text: Two people, equally hardworking and equally smart—why does one leave behind tens of millions and the other a pile of bills? Two men, equally hardworking and equally smart. Why did one leave millions behind, and the other a stack of unpaid bills? Rich Dad Poor Dad Rich Dad Poor Dad When Robert was nine, there were two dads in his life. One was his own father: a PhD who studied at Stanford, the University of Chicago, and Northwestern on full scholarships, and later became Hawaii's education official. The other was his friend Mike's dad: he never even finished eighth grade. When Robert was nine he had two dads. One was his own father: a Ph.D. who studied at Stanford, the University of Chicago and Northwestern on full scholarships, and later ran education for the state of Hawaii. The other was his best friend Mike's father, who never finished eighth grade. Both men worked hard, earned plenty, and had real influence. Yet the real dad worried about money all his life and left bills to be paid; Mike's dad became one of the richest men in Hawaii and left tens of millions to his family, charities, and the church. Both worked hard all their lives. Both earned good incomes. Both were strong, influential men. Yet his own father struggled with money and left bills to be paid. Mike's father became one of the richest men in Hawaii and left tens of millions to his family, to charities and to his church. The difference isn't on the paycheck; it's on their lips. items.text: Ten cents an hour, and later not a single penny — why did Rich Dad 'bully' two nine-year-olds like that? Ten cents an hour, and later nothing at all. Why did rich dad treat two nine-year-olds this way? Lesson 1: The Rich Don't Work for Money Lesson 1: The Rich Don't Work for Money Robert and Mike wanted to learn to make money. They first tried melting toothpaste tubes to cast coins, but were stopped by Robert's own dad: that's counterfeiting. So they went to ask Mike's dad. Rich Dad said: fine, come work at my supermarket on Saturdays, ten cents an hour, three hours a time. Robert and Mike wanted to learn how to make money. First they melted toothpaste tubes to cast coins, until Robert's dad stopped them — that is counterfeiting. So they asked Mike's dad. Rich dad said yes: work Saturdays at my store, three hours, ten cents an hour. Three weeks later, Robert had had enough. Three hours of work earned thirty cents, and a comic cost ten. He stormed into Rich Dad's office to quit, and threatened to report him for breaking child-labor laws. Rich Dad laughed: this is exactly the first lesson I wanted to teach you. Three weeks later Robert had had enough. Three hours of work bought thirty cents, and one comic cost ten. He marched into rich dad's office, furious, ready to quit and to report him for breaking child-labour laws. Rich dad smiled: this is exactly the first lesson. Rich Dad says most people spend their whole lives in this loop: get up, go to work, pay bills; get up, go to work, pay bills. items.text: Your family's house, your dad's car, your game console — which ones put money into your pocket, and which take it out? Your family's home, the car, your games console — which ones put money in your pocket, and which take it out? Lesson 2: Why Teach Financial Literacy Lesson 2: Why Teach Financial Literacy? Rich Dad said if the whole book kept just one rule, it would be this: tell assets from liabilities, then buy assets. His definition is almost too simple to be accounting: an asset puts money in your pocket, a liability takes money out. If only one rule survives from the whole book, rich dad said, it is this: know the difference between an asset and a liability, then buy assets. His definition is simpler than any accounting textbook: an asset puts money in your pocket, a liability takes money out. Why do adults keep getting something so simple wrong? Because people look at “what a thing is worth,” not “which direction the money flows.” A new car loses a quarter of its value the moment it leaves the dealership; a home you live in costs a mortgage, taxes, insurance, and roof repairs every month. On the ledger they're written as assets; in cash flow they're liabilities. Why do grown-ups get this so wrong? Because they look at what a thing is worth instead of which way the money flows. A new car loses about a quarter of its price the moment it leaves the lot. A home you live in eats mortgage payments, taxes, insurance and roof repairs every month. The students laughed — everyone knows you sell hamburgers. He said: no, my business is real estate. He explains: selling franchises is the surface; what really matters is each store's location. A franchisee buys not just a business but that piece of land. Today McDonald's owns more real estate than the Catholic Church, holding the world's most valuable intersections and street corners. items.excerpt: Why did the law to 'tax the rich' end up landing on the very people who voted for it?
items.text: Why did the law to 'tax the rich' end up landing on the very people who voted for it? Why did the tax that was sold as “make the rich pay” end up landing on the people who voted for it? Lesson 4: The History of Taxes and the Power of the Corporation Lesson 4: The History of Taxes and the Power of Corporations School teaches Robin Hood, robbing the rich to give to the poor, as a hero. Rich Dad said: Robin Hood is a robber. The author didn't understand then and only grasped it as an adult — he wasn't endorsing robbery; he was saying the idea of 'taking other people's money and dividing it up' usually ends up hurting ordinary people. At school Robin Hood was a hero who robbed the rich to give to the poor. Rich dad called him a crook. Robert only understood later: the point was not to approve of robbery, but that the idea of taking someone else's money to hand around usually ends up hurting ordinary people. History makes it clear. Britain and the U.S. originally had no standing income tax, only a temporary levy in wartime: Britain fought Napoleon in 1799–1816, the U.S. fought its Civil War in 1861–1865. In 1874 Britain made the income tax permanent, and in 1913 the U.S. did the same through the Sixteenth Amendment. History makes it clear. Britain and America originally had no permanent income tax, only temporary war taxes: Britain 1799–1816 against Napoleon, America 1861–1865 for the Civil War. The author says what holds most people back is never 'not knowing,' but fear of making mistakes, fear of losing money, fear of being laughed at. That's why the best students at school often aren't the ones who end up richest — because school rewards not making mistakes, while opportunity rewards daring to try and fail. This lesson is about courage. What stops most people, the author says, is not ignorance but fear — of mistakes, of losing money, of being laughed at. That is why the best students are often not the wealthiest adults: school rewards never being wrong, while opportunity rewards being willing to be wrong. He gives his own example: in Phoenix he bought a house listed at $60,000 for $20,000, using borrowed money for the down payment, then resold it at $60,000 and took back a $40,000 promissory note. Overcoming obstacles Overcoming Obstacles The author says even with a perfect score in financial knowledge, five things can still keep a person standing still. He calls them roadblocks. The first is fear: fear of losing money. He says fearing loss is right — everyone does; the difference is what you do after being afraid. Even someone with perfect financial literacy can be stopped by five things, the author says. He calls them obstacles. The first is fear of losing money. Fear is normal — everyone has it. The difference is what you do after you feel it. He used an analogy: Texans aren't afraid of losing—they're afraid of “not losing big enough.” Meaning: what makes people rich isn't never failing, but being able to stand up and try again after failing. He quotes an old saying: losers are those who've never won, and winners are those who lost but didn't stop. He uses a Texas saying: people there are not afraid of losing, they are afraid of losing too small. The point is that wealth comes not from never failing but from getting up after failure. items.title: He calculated every variable — except how much his conscience could bear
items.excerpt: The first book of Doudou's trilogy is often read as a business-war novel and then set aside. Do the math more carefully and it's actually a cold, clear post-mortem of a failure: an operator who accounted for every rule, every human motive, and every risk control lost to a variable he never put in the model—how much weight a conscience can bear.
items.text:
There's a kind of person who spends their whole life studying “how to win.”
Doudou's Betrayal is about just such a person.
The book came out in 2000 and was adapted the same year into a TV series of the same name, starring Xu Qing and Wei Zi. It's the first of Doudou's trilogy and the least discussed—because the later two have the big IP Tian Dao behind them, while Betrayal is treated by many as an ordinary business-crime novel: finish it, enjoy it, put it down.
But if you work through the book's numbers a little more carefully, you'll find it's actually a remarkably dispassionate post-mortem of a failure.
The subject of this post-mortem is an operator with extremely high intelligence, very deep resources, and an exquisitely designed chain.
He lost.
Lost to a variable he never put into the model.
That variable is: how much weight a conscience can bear.
I. A man who put himself in prison
The novel opens in an unusual way.
Song Yikun, general manager of Dongfang Architectural Decoration Engineering Company, was suddenly arrested. Everyone was shocked; everyone thought he'd simply had bad luck.
But read on and you realize this was no accident. He planned it himself.
The publisher's blurb gives three motives: escape disaster, preserve his strength, and—more than that—create a chance for divorce. And that so-called “disaster” in the novel has a concrete shape: Lin Feng, the bank credit-department director who once lent him money, embezzled 5.7 million in public funds and it came to light. It's a debt he can't repay and can't deny.
Look at the scale of this game—usually a person …

items.title: He Didn't Give That Village a Single Cent, Yet Turned the Whole Village Around
items.excerpt: The original novel behind 'Tiandao' (The Way of Heaven). Across the whole Wangmiao Village story, how much money did Ding Yuanying actually put in? Zero. What he gave wasn't money but rules, a market, and a whip — and he himself still had to climb Mount Wutai to ask for permission.
items.text:
In 2005, Doudou wrote a novel called 'The Distant Savior.'
It was later adapted into the TV series 'Tiandao' (The Way of Heaven). Nearly twenty years after it aired, its Douban rating has risen rather than fallen. But interestingly, almost all the discussion centers on how 'awesome' Ding Yuanying is and how 'profound' his lines are.
Very few people sit down and do the math.
Here's how the numbers work:Across the whole Wangmiao Village story, how much money did Ding Yuanying actually put in?
The answer is zero.
He never gave that village a single cent.
So what did he do? What he gave was worth far more than money—and far crueler.
Today isn't about how 'godlike' Ding Yuanying is; it's about the thing he did—perhaps the deepest thought experiment about 'help' in Chinese business fiction.
I. A hermit and a village
First, why Ding Yuanying turned up in that small city.
When Ding Yuanying ran a private fund in Berlin, he was a legendary figure in business. He brought the fund a net profit of 42.8 million marks, of which he took 5.136 million.
Then he stopped of his own accord. The novel is vague about why he withdrew, saying only it was 'for reasons of personal condition and capital safety,' plus one matter he 'was unwilling to discuss with foreigners.'
The outcome he accepted: funds frozen for two to three years, and a five-year ban from the same industry. There was originally also 180,000 marks in compensation attached—he struck that item out.
What he had left in the end was 136,000 marks. That was his entire living expenses in Gucheng.
He rented the top floor—the fifth—with no…

items.title: He gave back a 500,000 bonus, asked only for four words, and finally died in Moscow
items.excerpt: Before he died, Luo Jiaming already held the right answer: see the road but don't walk it. He died anyway. The last book of the trilogy isn't about how to find a path; it's about what else you buy when you copy a ready-made one—exemption from responsibility.
items.text:
On the night of August 24, 1991, in Moscow, a Chinese businessman fired a gun — and the person he killed was himself.
His name is Luo Jiaming. The novel begins on the night he dies.
This man was originally a businessman in Beijing, then moved his whole family to New York and opened a Chinese restaurant called “Yuxiangge.” Later he sold his Beijing property, mortgaged the New York restaurant too, and bet everything on Russian oil fields, holding drilling rights to 150 wells.
In August 1991, the August Coup collapsed; the Soviet officials he had leaned on were arrested one after another, and his extraction rights were confiscated. Within three days everything went to zero, with huge debts coming due on top of it all.
Doudou's 'Tianmu Hongchen' (2013, the last volume of the trilogy) begins with this very funeral.
And the truly sharp edge of this book is: before Luo Jiaming died, he was already holding the right answer.
He died anyway.
One: where did those four characters come from
The bond between Luo Jiaming and Ye Zinong is unfolded in the book through the widow Lin Xuehong's retelling.
Years ago, when Ye Zinong was poor, he borrowed 50,000 yuan from Luo Jiaming and promised him a return. A year later Ye Zinong had earned over two million and came to him carrying 500,000.
Luo Jiaming turned down the 500,000. He made just one request: if you truly want to thank me, give me one sentence worth more than 500,000.
Ye Zinong thought for a moment, took out the four treasures of the study, and wrote four characters: Don't Walk the Beaten Path.
I read this passage three times.

items.title: A Decade of Life: turn your days into a project
items.excerpt: Health, language, investing, AI—four domains, one dataset, a ten-year scale. Why I built myself a workbench, and what really separates "practice" from "planning."
items.text:
After thirty, one thing has become clearer and clearer to me:Between knowing and doing lies an entire system.
Most of the books you've read, the goals you've declared, and the tutorials you've bookmarked never became part of your life. It isn't a willpower problem; it's a feedback problem — no record, no feedback; no feedback, and sticking with it runs entirely on mood.
So I built myself a "Life Decade" workbench: treat ten years as a project to manage—four domains, one dataset, a weekly review.
Four areas
Health: sleep, heart rate, exercise. Let the wristband's data do the talking, not 'I feel like I've been doing okay lately.'
Language: A little foreign-language input and output every day, advancing by milestones—not congratulating yourself for “how long you've studied.”
Investing: ETF grids, pension backtests, A-share reviews. Backtest first, then bet; work out the worst case first, then talk returns.
AI: Weave AI into your daily workflow—collecting, organizing, distilling insights, and reminding—so the machines handle the repetitive work.
What the workspace looks like
Technically it's a three-piece stack: a Rust backend handles storage and computation (grid backtests, pension simulations — the parts that need to be fast), a React frontend handles the dashboard and milestones, and Python scripts bring in outside data — health metrics, market quotes, LLM-generated insights — writing it all to disk on a daily schedule.
All the data lives in local JSON files, with no cloud dependency. I want this thing to still run ten years from now, instead of being buried the day some pr…

items.title: The barbell: one end extremely safe, the other extremely risky
items.excerpt: Thales put down a small deposit and rented every olive press — a big win if right, a small loss if wrong. The barbell strategy isn't 50/50 but 90/10: the large portion extremely safe, the small portion extremely bold, the middle ground the most dangerous.
items.text:
My favorite story in Antifragile takes place in ancient Greece more than two thousand years ago.
Thales and the Olive Presses
The philosopher Thales knew astronomy and predicted a bumper olive harvest the following year. So in winter, at a very low price, he rented the use of every olive press nearby. The next year the harvest really was abundant, everyone needed presses, and he sublet them at a high price, making a fortune.
What if the prediction is wrong? He loses only that small deposit—he won't go bankrupt.
This is:Spend a little money to buy a chance that "pays off big if it happens."
The barbell strategy
A barbell is heavy at both ends and light in the middle. Taleb says resources should be placed the same way:
One end extremely safe: Put most of your resources where things almost never go wrong.
One end: extremely risky: Put a small slice of resources where losing doesn't matter and winning is huge.
The middle zone — 'looks safe, but hard to pin down' — is the most dangerous of all. So-called 'medium risk' is often risk underestimated and upside capped off: it belongs to neither end.
Note the ratio: the barbell isn't 50/50, but90 to 10. The big side is extremely safe, the small side extremely bold.
Optionality and Convexity
With the deposit, Thales bought the right to decide whether to use the olive presses next yearOptionality— you can take it or leave it. Its advantage: you don't need to predict accurately; you only need 'big gains when right, small losses when wrong.'
Taleb uses “convexity” to describe this shape:Losses limited, gains potentially large. The opposi…

items.title: The turkey's one thousand and first day
items.excerpt: The turkey logged 1,000 days of evidence that 'humans love me'; day 1,001 was Thanksgiving. That things have always been this way doesn't mean they always will be—this is the Black Swan's gentlest and sharpest lesson.
items.text:
This is"Not Afraid of Uncertainty"The story in Lesson 4 is also the one I tell friends most often.
A Story
There was a turkey living on a farm. Every day at 11 a.m. the farmer came to feed it. The turkey was clever and started keeping records: “Day 1, food; Day 2, food... Day 1000, food.”
It reaches a conclusion: 'Humans love me; they will keep feeding me forever.'
Day 1,001 was Thanksgiving.
The three traits of a Black Swan
Taleb gave “Black Swan events” three features:
Surprises: in past experience, you can find no evidence that it must happen.
Big impact: Once it happens, the impact is enormous.
Explainable after the fact: After it happens, people always concoct a story saying, "I knew it all along."
The name 'Black Swan' comes from a true story: Europeans saw millions of white swans and concluded that 'all swans are white'—until the first black swan was spotted in Australia, and a thousand-year belief was overturned by a single observation.
The Turkey Problem
The turkey's mistake wasn't “trusting experience,” butUsing past experience to predict a world whose rules may suddenly change. Every meal reinforces its false belief. The more data it collects, the more confident — and the more fragile — it becomes.
Taleb doesn't mean 'don't trust experience,' but this: experience is reliable only in a world where 'the rules don't change.' In the real world, the rules do change.
Put it into daily life
You've always used the 'copy it out three times' method, and your grades are fine. Change the teacher, change the question type, and the method can suddenly stop working.

items.title: Dynamic Hedging: A Craft for "Manufacturing Insurance"
items.excerpt: A 460-page trader's manual that is really about the craft of manufacturing insurance: options are the policies, the Greeks are the dashboard, and dynamic hedging is adjusting your position day by day so volatility doesn't bite you.
items.text:
Taleb's *Dynamic Hedging* is a 460-page trader's manual, subtitled 'Managing Vanilla and Exotic Options.' Many are scared off by the formulas, but once you read it down to its bones, the whole book is about just one thing:
An option is like an insurance policy. The market maker sells the insurance, collects the premium, then buys and sells the underlying every day so price swings don't 'bite' him. That daily adjusting of the position is called dynamic hedging.
I turned this book into 16 general-education lessons,Dynamic Hedging · Even Kids Can Understand. This piece explains the skeleton of the whole book.
Options: a 'regret pill'
The best analogy for an option is a deposit on a house. You like a 3-million-yuan home, put down 100,000, and agree that six months from now you have the right to buy at 3 million:
The price rises to 3.5 million: exercise the right, buy at 3 million, and net 400,000.
If the price drops to 2.5 million: just don't buy—the most you lose is the 100,000 deposit.
The 100,000 deposit is the premium, 3 million is the strike price, and six months later is the expiration date. The most important point:The buyer has the right but not the obligation; the seller has the obligation but not the right.
Hence the maxim: buy options and risk is limited while upside can be unlimited; sell options and upside is limited while risk can be unlimited. Selling options is like being an insurance company—most policies never pay out, so premiums are profit; but you make small money most of the time and pay out big when things go wrong.

items.title: Turning Taleb's Incerto series into 12 lessons for children
items.excerpt: Five thick books really answer just one question: the world loves to change its face without warning — what should we do? I broke them into 12 lessons, 32 cards, and a 21-day review schedule, and here I'll explain how the course was designed.
items.text:
After finishing Taleb's five-book Incerto series last year — 'Fooled by Randomness,' 'The Black Swan,' 'Antifragile,' 'Skin in the Game,' and 'The Bed of Procrustes' — the first thing I did wasn't write a review, but think:Can any of this be explained to a ten-year-old?
Not watered down into chicken-soup inspiration, but actually teaching him three things: don't be fooled by luck, grow stronger with every fall, and don't let others take the hits for you. Hence this course:Learning "Not Afraid of Uncertainty" from Taleb, 12 lessons, 25 minutes each, easy enough even for a grade-schooler.
Five books are a band
This set of books looks thick, but it's really answering just one question:
The world loves to change its face without warning — what should we do about it?
Taleb's answer isn't 'calculate exactly when it will change face,' but three things:
Don't be fooled by luck— See the dice hidden behind success.
Don't fear the market changing its face — even turn it to your advantage— Become someone who grows stronger with every fall.
Don't let others take the hits for you— Whoever makes the decision bears the consequences.
Each of the five books handles one stretch: *Fooled by Randomness* sees through luck, *The Black Swan* recognizes sudden jumps, *Antifragile* makes you stronger, *Skin in the Game* is about acting and being, and *The Bed of Procrustes* keeps you from cramming the world into ready-made frames.
I'd suggest ordering the learning as 'first see through, then grow strong, finally learn to be a person' — like the three steps of growing up: open your eyes, train your b…

items.text:
Trading for a Living talks about a lot of indicators, but really it's answering just one question:How does an ordinary person make a living from trading without being swallowed by the market?
Elder's answer rests on three pillars: manage yourself (psychology), read the crowd (method), protect your capital (money management). And *The Art of Selling* supplies the other half: a good buyer is still an apprentice; only a good seller is a master. This course combines the two books into 21 lessons of about 25 minutes each, built on five steps — story, keywords, everyday examples, three questions, and 'explain it to someone else' — so that even elementary schoolers can understand.
Course Structure (Nine Modules)
Module One · Managing Yourself(Lessons 1–3): surfing without drowning; greed, fear and hope; the inner coach and journal — start by admitting you'll make mistakes.
Module 2 · Reading the Market(Lessons 4–5): price is a crowd voting; trend, support and resistance; candlesticks and channels — behind the price is human behavior.
Module 3 · A Checkup for the Market(Lessons 6–8): moving averages; MACD histogram and KD/RSI; volume and the advance-decline line — take the market's temperature with indicators.
Module 4 · Elder's Tools(Lessons 9–10): the Force Index; Elder-Ray and the Parabolic; the Triple Screen — a few weapons of Elder's own.
Module 5 · Buying and Grading(Lessons 11–12): three buying choices; channel grades A/B/C/D; two strategies with a trading worksheet — grade first, then place the order.

items.title: Learn 'The Road of Trading' with Chen Kai
items.excerpt: Turning Chen Kai's The Trading Path: How to Build Your Own Investment System into 21 lessons even a grade-schooler can follow: 40 knowledge cards, 9 module challenges, a 20-question final exam, and a 21-day review schedule.
items.text:
The Trading Road covers a lot of technique, but really it answers just one question:How do you survive the market and build a trading system of your own?
Chen Kai's answer isn't 'find a move that always wins.' It is: first understand the market and your opponent, then understand yourself, fit the safety valve of a stop-loss, and finally fold short-term trading, long-term holding, and arbitrage into a system of your own. This course breaks the book's 14 chapters into 21 lessons of about 25 minutes each, using five parts — a story, key terms, real-life examples, three questions, and 'teach it to someone else' — so even a grade-schooler can follow.
Course Structure (Nine Modules)
Module 1 · Understanding the Market (Lessons 1–4): A big map of the market, the four schools of trading, five maxims and three magic mirrors, trading frameworks and the code of price action.
Module 2 · Understanding Yourself(Lessons 5–6): know yourself, trading and life — the circle of competence and the shared root of profit and loss.
Module 3 · Learning Not to Lose Big(Lessons 7–8): why you lose money, and the stop-loss / take-profit safety valves — first learn not to lose everything.
Module 4 · Reading Your Opponent(Lessons 9–10): the market zoo and the retail trader's evolutionary path — knowing who you are trading against.
Module Five · Short-Term Skills (Lessons 11–13): Intraday charts and the order book, ultra-short-term craft, cycle resonance and macro sentiment.
Module Six · The Language of Charts(Lesson 14): Candlesticks and divergence—read the diary price has written.

items.title: Dynamic Hedging · Even Kids Can Understand
items.excerpt: Turn Taleb's 460-page trader's manual Dynamic Hedging into 16 lessons even elementary-school kids can grasp: options, the Greeks, dynamic hedging, exotic options, and tail risk—with a glossary, a formula cheat sheet, and a 30-question comprehensive quiz.
items.text:
*Dynamic Hedging* appears to be about options, but it is really about the craft of 'manufacturing insurance': the market maker sells insurance, collects the premium, then buys and sells the underlying every day so price swings can't bite him. That daily adjustment of the position is dynamic hedging.
This course doesn't memorize formulas; it first makes sense of four things:What options are, where their prices come from, where the risk hides, and how to survive.
Four Stages
Phase One · First understand the 'insurance policy': Options as a regret pill, the four kinds of people in the market, and the three-layer cake of price.
Stage 2 · Learning to 'drive this car': Delta is the steering wheel, Gamma the bump magnifier, Vega the weather forecast, Theta the rent on time—and dynamic hedging means building your own insurance.
Stage 3 · Reading the 'special insurance clauses': The truth about volatility, in two lessons on exotic options.
Stage Four · Becoming a Risk Manager Who "Lives Long": The wisdom of risk management, the master's toolkit, and a full review.
Appendices and Self-Tests
Appendix A: a bilingual glossary so you won't get lost against the original book.
Appendix B: a cheat sheet of formulas, keeping only the most useful ones.
Appendix C: a 30-question comprehensive quiz covering all 16 lessons.
The one line for the whole book
The real difficulty isn't “can you compute,” but that volatility shifts, correlations shift, liquidity vanishes, and extreme events fall outside the model. So living long matters more than computing precisely.

items.title: Learning "Not Afraid of Uncertainty" from Taleb
items.excerpt: Turn Fooled by Randomness, The Black Swan, Antifragile, Skin in the Game and Wisdom and Spells into 12 lessons even a primary-school child can follow: 32 knowledge cards, module challenges, a 20-question final exam and a 21-day review schedule.
items.text:
This set of books looks thick, but it's really answering just one question:The world loves to change its face without warning — what should we do about it?
Taleb's answer isn't 'calculate exactly when it will change face.' It is three things: don't be fooled by luck; don't fear the change of face, even use it; and don't let someone else take the blow for you. This course breaks five books into 12 lessons of about 25 minutes each, using five segments—story, keywords, a life example, three questions, and “explain it to someone else”—so even a grade-schooler can learn these three things.
Course Structure
Module 1 · Learning to Doubt First(Fooled by Randomness): luck versus skill, survivorship bias, ergodicity—winning many times is not as good as never being wiped out once.
Module Two · Getting to Know a World That Changes Its Face(*Black Swan*): the turkey's 1,001 days, Mediocristan and Extremistan, and the narrative fallacy.
Module Three · Getting Stronger with Every Fall(Antifragile): the glass cup, the iron box, and muscle; good intentions doing harm; the barbell strategy; subtraction and time.
Module Four · Doing Things and Being a Person(Skin in the Game, The Bed of Procrustes): skin in the game; never push yourself to the point of no next time.
Companion tools
32 knowledge cards: flip to memorize, mark “needs more practice,” quiz yourself anytime.
4 module challenges + a 20-question final exam: grade yourself; answering wrong and saying so out loud is worth more than memorizing the right answer.
21-Day Review Schedule: spaced repetition, check off each day, progress save…
